title: Sequences and Series
tagline: Year 3 — Pattern finding, nth term, sum of special series and difference-of-differences methods

introduction.overview: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers following a rule; a series is the sum of its terms. This chapter teaches how to find the rule (first differences, second differences, ratios), how to write the nth term, and how to sum the standard series: natural numbers, squares, cubes, odd and even numbers. These tools feed the next chapters on AP, GP and mixed progressions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Missing-term and nth-term questions are common in aptitude papers and in number-series rounds.
introduction.realWorldContext: Repayment schedules, population patterns and pattern recognition in data all use sequences.

learningObjectives: Find the rule of a sequence using differences and ratios
Write the nth term of a pattern
Sum 1 + 2 + … + n, squares, cubes, odd and even numbers
Use the second-difference method for quadratic patterns

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Terms are written T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ.

coreDefinitions: Sequence: an ordered list with a rule for each term.
Series: the sum of the terms of a sequence.
First difference: Tₖ₊₁ − Tₖ. Second difference: the difference of first differences.
Constant first difference means an arithmetic pattern; constant ratio means a geometric pattern.
Constant second difference means the nth term is a quadratic in n.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Look at how the terms change. If the change is constant, it is linear. If the change itself changes by a constant, it is quadratic. If the terms multiply by a constant, it is geometric.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write the first differences, then the second differences, then the ratios. The first level that becomes constant reveals the rule.

mainNarrative: To find a rule, write the differences. For 3, 7, 11, 15 the first difference is always 4, so the nth term is 4n − 1.
If the first differences are not constant, take second differences. For 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 the first differences are 4, 6, 8, 10 and the second differences are all 2, so the nth term is n² + n.
If the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, the sequence is geometric. 3, 6, 12, 24 has ratio 2 and nth term 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹.
Mixed patterns alternate two rules. In 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 the terms at odd places go 2, 4, 8 (doubling) and those at even places go 3, 6, 12 (doubling). Split the sequence into its interleaved parts.

deepDiveAspects.title: Differences of squares
deepDiveAspects.content: The sequence n² has first differences 2n + 1, which are the odd numbers, and second difference 2.

deepDiveAspects.title: Sum from the nth term
deepDiveAspects.content: The sum of terms from the m-th to the n-th is Sₙ − Sₘ₋₁.

solvedExamples.title: Sum of cubes
solvedExamples.question: Find 1³ + 2³ + … + 9³.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Square of the sum of naturals.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Sum of cubes equals the square of the sum.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Constant first difference ⇒ linear; constant second difference ⇒ quadratic; constant ratio ⇒ geometric.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping at one level of differences
Mixing sum of cubes and sum of squares

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Test the formula for n = 1 and n = 2.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Check three terms before trusting a rule.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Series questions are pattern recognition plus a standard formula.

easy.question: The next term in 3, 7, 11, 15, … is
easy.explanation: The common difference is 4, so the next term is 15 + 4 = 19.

intermediate.question: The next term in 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, … is
intermediate.explanation: The terms are n(n + 1), so the 6th term is 6 × 7 = 42.

advanced.question: The next term in 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, … is
advanced.explanation: Even places 3, 6, 12 and odd places 2, 4, 8, 16 each double, so the next term is 16.

advanced.question: The sum 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 99 equals
advanced.explanation: There are 50 odd numbers, so the sum is 50² = 2500.

placementStyle.question: The nth term of 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, … is
placementStyle.explanation: The terms are (n + 1)² − 1 = n² + 2n; check n = 1 gives 3.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the nth term of a quadratic pattern?
Can I recall the three standard sums?
